questions.q: Why does this course skip solving the Schrödinger equation for the hydrogen atom?
options: Because hydrogen atom calculations are too difficult to be taught correctly
Because a qubit's Hilbert space is a clean, finite-dimensional abstraction engineered by hardware teams, so software built on gates never needs to re-derive it from a continuous atomic potential
Because the hydrogen atom has no energy levels worth studying
Because this course covers the hydrogen atom in a later chapter instead
questions.explain: Hydrogen-atom Schrödinger-equation solutions matter for predicting atomic spectra and chemistry, not for reasoning about qubits — hardware teams already engineer qubits to have a clean finite-dimensional Hilbert space, so software-level quantum computing never needs that derivation.

questions.q: Why is perturbation theory left out of this course's scope?
options: Because quantum gates are exact, discrete unitary operations you specify directly, not approximations to some underlying continuous Hamiltonian that need a perturbative approximation
Because perturbation theory was proven incorrect
Because perturbation theory is only used in classical mechanics
Because this course replaces perturbation theory with angular momentum coupling instead
questions.explain: Perturbation theory approximates real systems whose Hamiltonian is close to an exactly-solvable one. Quantum gates in computing are exact, discrete unitary operations defined directly — there's no messy real-world Hamiltonian to approximate, so the toolkit has no role here.

questions.q: Which of the following IS explicitly within this course's scope, according to the lesson?
options: Path integrals as Feynman's sum-over-trajectories formulation
Unitary evolution, because every quantum logic gate is a unitary operator
Angular momentum coupling for multi-particle atomic spin addition
Perturbation theory for approximating atomic energy shifts
questions.explain: Unitary evolution is explicitly in scope because gates are unitary operators — the direct bridge from postulate 5 to how circuits work. Path integrals, angular momentum coupling, and perturbation theory are all explicitly named as out of scope.

questions.q: What single fact does the lesson identify as the "hinge" explaining why this finite-dimensional subset of QM is exactly right for computing?
options: That light behaves as both a wave and a particle

That a quantum circuit is nothing but a sequence of unitary operators applied to a finite-dimensional state vector, followed by measurement — pure linear algebra, with no differential equations or specific physical potentials needed
That atoms emit discrete spectral lines
That classical bits are deterministic
questions.explain: The lesson's central argument is that circuits are built entirely from unitary operators on a finite-dimensional space plus measurement — a purely linear-algebra structure that needs none of the continuous, perturbative, or atomic-physics machinery a physics-major curriculum requires.

questions.q: Why does the lesson argue that skipping topics like the hydrogen atom and perturbation theory is a deliberate scope choice rather than a loss of rigor?
options: Because those topics are taught later in this same course, just under different names

Because every topic this course does cover (postulates, Dirac notation, superposition, measurement, entanglement, unitary evolution, no-cloning) is taught to the same standard of precision a physics major gets, with no hand-waving — the difference is which topics make the cut, not how rigorously included ones are treated
Because rigor doesn't matter for software engineers
Because physics majors don't actually need rigor either
questions.explain: The lesson is explicit that the included topics get full textbook-level precision; what's different from a physics-major sequence is the selection of topics, chosen because they are necessary and sufficient for reasoning about qubits, gates, and algorithms — not a watering-down of what remains.
